title: Does Thematic Require Manual Theme Tuning?
summary: No. Thematic builds themes with no rules to write and refreshes coverage monthly on its own. New themes go to a human for approval by design.
body_markdown:
Anyone[evaluating feedback analytics](https://getthematic.com/insights/ai-powered-customer-feedback-theme-discovery) eventually hits the maintenance question. A tool can look impressive in a demo and still cost an analyst two days a month once the theme taxonomy drifts from what customers are actually talking about. Competitors raise it directly. Enterpret's comparison page states that "Thematic's theme structures require manual tuning and updates." It's a fair question, and it deserves a specific answer rather than a denial.


The short answer: Thematic does not require manual theme tuning to produce accurate themes, and it does require a human decision before a new theme enters a live analysis. Those two facts aren't in tension. Thematic builds a two-level taxonomy of themes and subthemes from your feedback, with no rules, keyword lists, or pre-training to write. It keeps that taxonomy's coverage current through a scheduled monthly workflow that applies new matching phrases to existing themes without asking anyone. What Thematic deliberately doesn't do is add new themes to a live analysis on its own. A new theme changes the shape of every report built on it, so it goes to a named reviewer for approval.


That review gate is the part competitors describe as a tuning burden. It's closer to the opposite.


## What "theme tuning" actually means


Theme tuning gets used for four different jobs, and vendors blur them because the blur is useful.


- **Building the taxonomy.** Deciding which themes exist, from the feedback rather than from a guess.
- **Maintaining coverage.** Making sure new feedback keeps matching the themes you already have, as customers change vocabulary.
- **Restructuring.** Merging duplicates, moving misplaced subthemes, deleting themes too vague to act on.
- **Approving new themes.** Deciding whether an emerging pattern is a real theme or noise.


Only the last two involve judgment. The first two are mechanical, and a platform that makes you do them by hand is charging an analyst's salary for pattern matching. When a vendor says a competitor "requires manual tuning," ask which of the four they mean.


## What keeping a feedback taxonomy accurate actually requires


Taxonomies decay for a reason that has nothing to do with the tool. The language changes. A[review of concept drift in text stream mining](https://arxiv.org/html/2312.02901v1) puts it plainly: "In text streams, concept drift occurs when the underlying patterns and relationships within the textual data shift, making previously learned models or approaches ineffective." A theme set built in January on shipping complaints won't match October's vocabulary about a new delivery partner.


Three things have to happen for a taxonomy to keep up:


- **Coverage expands as vocabulary changes.** New phrasings map to the theme you already have instead of sitting untagged.
- **Emerging topics surface early.** A new issue is worth catching in the month it appears, not the quarter after.
- **Structure stays clean.** Overlapping themes accumulate, splitting the volume for one issue across three themes and making it look smaller than it is.


Doing all three by hand is the real cost. Thematic's own 2022 guide to[building a feedback taxonomy](https://getthematic.com/insights/how-to-build-a-customer-feedback-taxonomy) describes exactly that arrangement, down to a named taxonomy owner watching for emerging themes. It predates every automation described below. Forrester's[Total Economic Impact study of Thematic](https://getthematic.com/assets/downloads/TEI_Thematic_2023.pdf) , published in June 2023, put manual data prep, reading, and tagging at 4,250 hours eliminated for its composite organization. A research director in that study described the before state: "I simply wouldn't have the time to sit there and read 20,000 responses to derive insights."


## Where most feedback tools fall short


- **Rules and keyword lists.** Rules need a person to write and rewrite them. Thematic measures rule-based approaches at roughly[60 to 70 percent accuracy](https://getthematic.com/insights/ai-feedback-analytics-accuracy) , against 80 to 90 percent for its own themes before any human refinement.
- **Fixed taxonomies.** A pre-built industry taxonomy needs no maintenance because it never adapts. It also never tells you anything specific to your product.
- **Black-box themes.** If you can't see how a theme was built, you can't correct it or defend the number to a stakeholder who disagrees.
- **All-or-nothing automation.** A tool that applies every change on its own leaves you explaining last quarter's report against a taxonomy that changed underneath it.


## How Thematic handles theme upkeep


**Themes come from your feedback, not from you.** Thematic builds a two-level taxonomy of themes and subthemes from the data you connect, with no rules to write. Add a channel later and Thematic links your existing themes to it rather than starting over.


**Coverage maintenance runs monthly and applies itself.** Thematic offers a Theme Maintenance workflow, configured per lens. Its in-product description is direct: "Expands the phrases mapped to your existing themes so new feedback keeps matching. Changes are applied automatically each month." It works over the previous month's feedback and applies the changes to the live theme set. A named recipient gets an informational email. No action is required.


**New theme discovery surfaces candidates for approval.** The same workflow can surface themes emerging in the previous month's feedback. Those aren't applied. They arrive as a review request with approve or deny per proposal, because introducing a new theme changes the shape of every analysis built on it. Candidates are pushed to the named recipient, so nobody is checking each upload by hand for new topics.


**Restructuring is proposed for you, one click to stage.**[Thematic's Themes Editor](https://getthematic.com/insights/customize-ai-themes-customer-feedback) runs 18 evaluation checks across your theme hierarchy and your untagged comments: 12 structural checks and 6 discovery checks, each at three context levels. It returns a prioritized list of suggestions in six categories:


1. Overlapping themes that should merge.
2. Subthemes filed under the wrong parent.
3. Merged themes sitting in the wrong place.
4. Themes too generic to act on.
5. Untagged comments matching an existing theme.
6. Comment clusters warranting a new theme.


Each suggestion is applied or dismissed with a single click, which stages the change into a themes draft.


**The taxonomy stays inspectable throughout.** Atlassian's research team had previously spent six weeks[manually categorizing qualitative data](https://getthematic.com/insights/coding-qualitative-data) and still covered only a fraction of its dataset. It chose Thematic partly because the[white-box model](https://getthematic.com/insights/how-atlassian-built-a-scalable-data-pipeline/) let its analysts validate patterns and refine categories rather than accept them on faith.


## What still needs a person


Two things, and both are deliberate.


**A new theme waits for approval.** Coverage expansion applies itself. Introducing a brand new theme does not, because a new theme changes the shape of every analysis built on it. Each proposal is approved or denied by a person before it lands.


**Suggestions are proposals, not instructions.** Thematic's documentation is direct about the reason: "The AI doesn't have your business context, so a suggestion that looks reasonable may not fit your analytical goals." The one-click accept exists so the judgment is fast, not so it can be skipped.


Neither is a tuning loop. One is a governance gate. The other is a review queue.


## How teams run Thematic without a tuning loop


[Community Health System](https://getthematic.com/insights/community-health-systems-actionable-insights) , a not-for-profit healthcare network in California's central San Joaquin Valley, used Thematic on open-ended employee engagement responses across 250 departments. It produced 250 department reports in three days, work that had previously taken weeks. That saved more than 160 hours per survey cycle. "The only reason we built these single-page reports is because we had Thematic," said Alexandra Clifton, Organizational Development Partner. "Before, we were doing everything in an Excel spreadsheet."


At Greyhound, manual analysis of post-trip survey feedback had been roughly 80 percent of one analyst's job. Senior Customer Insights Analyst Matthew Schoolfield says Thematic "reduces my analytics time tenfold."


LendingTree analyzes more than 20,000 open-ended NPS comments every 90 days across seven product verticals. Lee King, its Head of Insights, says Thematic "worked straight out of the box" and "delivers the best quality of insights from text comments at scale." Both are claims about a running program, not a demo.


## What to ask every vendor about theme maintenance


Ask every vendor on your shortlist:


1. Are themes derived from my data, or selected from a fixed taxonomy?
2. Do I have to write or maintain rules or keyword lists?
3. When customer vocabulary changes, what expands theme coverage, and does it need me?
4. What happens when a genuinely new topic appears? Who is told, and who approves it?
5. Can I see how a theme was built, and can I correct it?
6. How do duplicate or misplaced themes get cleaned up, and by whom?
7. What is your theme accuracy before any human refinement, and after?
8. If a taxonomy change lands, can I tell which reports it affected?


## The short answer


Thematic does not require manual theme tuning. Themes are built from your feedback with no rules to write. Coverage maintenance runs on a monthly schedule that applies new phrase matches to existing themes on its own. What Thematic asks a person to do is approve new themes before they enter a live analysis, and decide which structural cleanups to accept. That's governance, not a tuning burden. It's the difference between a taxonomy you can defend in a stakeholder meeting and one that changed under you without telling you.


The test to run: put a shortlisted tool on last quarter's feedback and this quarter's, and ask who noticed the difference.
